subject: anaesthesia
title: Airway Anatomy, Direct Laryngoscopy, and Rapid Sequence Induction

steps.title: Laryngeal Functional Anatomy
steps.tx: **Laryngeal cartilage functional anatomy** consists of nine cartilages: three single (thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis) and three paired (arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform). The cricoid cartilage is the only completely circular cartilaginous ring in the respiratory tract, forming the narrowest anatomical point of the upper airway in infants and young children (subglottic space), whereas the vocal cord glottic chink represents the narrowest opening in adults.

steps.title: Macintosh versus Miller Blades
steps.tx: **Laryngoscope blade mechanical design** dictates distinct techniques of glottic visualization: the curved Macintosh blade is inserted along the right side of the mouth, sweeping the tongue leftward into the mandibular floor, with its tip seated into the vallecula to indirectly elevate the epiglottis via tension on the hyoepiglottic ligament. In contrast, the straight Miller blade directly scoops under and lifts the epiglottis, preferred in infants.

left.title: Curved Macintosh Blade
points: Tip placed into vallecula anterior to epiglottis
Indirect elevation of epiglottis preserves sensory nerve
Less vagal stimulation and trauma in adult patients

right.title: Straight Miller Blade
points: Tip directly scoops under and lifts the epiglottis
Presents direct view of glottic opening in narrow oropharynx
Preferred in neonates with floppy, elongated epiglottis

steps.title: Cormack-Lehane Laryngoscopy Grading
steps.tx: **Cormack-Lehane laryngoscopic view classification** grades glottic exposure during direct laryngoscopy without external laryngeal manipulation: Grade I visualizes the entire glottic aperture; Grade II visualizes only the posterior portion of vocal cords and arytenoids; Grade III visualizes only the epiglottis with zero glottic opening visible; and Grade IV reveals only the soft palate, with neither epiglottis nor vocal cords discernible.

steps.title: Endotracheal Tube Sizing and Depth
steps.tx: **Endotracheal tube sizing rules** specify internal diameter (ID) in millimeters: standard adult females take a 7.0 to 7.5 mm ID tube, secured at 21 centimeters at the corner of the incisors, while adult males take an 8.0 to 8.5 mm ID tube, secured at 23 centimeters. In children over one year, uncuffed tube size is calculated by (Age divided by 4) plus 4, whereas modern cuffed tubes use (Age divided by 4) plus 3.5.

steps.title: Endotracheal Cuff Pressure Limits
steps.tx: **Endotracheal tube cuff pressure limits** must be maintained strictly between 20 and 30 cmH2O (15 to 22 mmHg) utilizing a handheld aneroid manometer. Cuff pressures exceeding 30 cmH2O surpass capillary perfusion pressure of the tracheal mucosa, provoking ischemic ulceration, mucosal sloughing, and tracheal stenosis, whereas pressures under 20 cmH2O permit silent microaspiration of pharyngeal secretions around cuff folds.

left.title: Cuff Pressure >30 cmH2O
points: Exceeds tracheal mucosal capillary arteriolar pressure (30 cmH2O)
Tracheal mucosal ischemia, ulceration, and necrosis
Long-term scar contraction causing post-intubation tracheal stenosis

right.title: Cuff Pressure <20 cmH2O
points: Insufficient mechanical seal against tracheal wall
Ventilator gas leaks during positive-pressure inspiration
Permits silent microaspiration of colonized subglottic secretions

steps.title: Confirming Tracheal Tube Placement
steps.tx: **Confirmation of tracheal tube placement** demands immediate waveform capnography: persistence of continuous, rectangular carbon dioxide waveforms for at least five to six consecutive breaths serves as the unequivocal gold standard. Secondary clinical confirmation includes bilateral chest expansion, five-point auscultation (bilateral axillae, apices, and epigastrium to exclude stomach gurgling), tube fogging, and fiberoptic bronchoscopic visualization of tracheal cartilaginous rings and carina.

steps.title: Rapid Sequence Induction Steps
steps.tx: **Rapid sequence induction protocol** prevents pulmonary aspiration in patients with a full stomach, bowel obstruction, active reflux, or trauma. Key steps comprise preoxygenation with 100 percent oxygen for three minutes (or eight vital capacity breaths), administering a predetermined intravenous induction dose (propofol 2 mg/kg or ketamine 2 mg/kg) immediately followed by rapid-onset muscle relaxant (succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg or rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg), and withholding positive-pressure mask ventilation.

steps.title: Cricoid Pressure Application
steps.tx: **Sellick manoeuvre cricoid pressure** compresses the cartilaginous cricoid ring posteriorly against the sixth cervical vertebral body, occluding the compliant cervical esophagus to prevent passive regurgitation of gastric contents. A force of 10 Newtons is applied while the patient remains conscious, increasing to 30 Newtons (approximately 3 kilograms of force) upon loss of consciousness, maintained continuously until the endotracheal tube cuff is inflated and verified in the trachea.

left.title: Proper Cricoid Pressure (Sellick)
points: Downward posterior pressure on complete cricoid ring
Ten Newtons awake, increasing to 30 Newtons upon sleep
Occludes upper esophagus without distorting laryngeal cords

right.title: BURP Manoeuvre (Airway Optimization)
points: Backward, Upward, Rightward Pressure on thyroid cartilage
